title: Chapter 8 Mastery Quiz: Emotion, Motivation, Stress & Psychopathology
description: Test your mastery of the mesolimbic dopamine pathway, wanting vs. liking, chronic stress remodeling, biological models of depression and schizophrenia, and BCIs.

questions.question: Where are the dopaminergic cell bodies of the mesolimbic reward pathway located in the human brain?

options.text: Ventral Tegmental Area (VTA) in the midbrain
Locus Coeruleus in the pons
Pineal gland
Caudate nucleus

questions.explanation: The mesolimbic pathway originates in the midbrain Ventral Tegmental Area (VTA) and projects to the nucleus accumbens.

questions.question: What primary brain region receives dense dopaminergic projections from the VTA to mediate incentive salience and motivation?

options.text: Nucleus Accumbens (NAc)
Primary visual cortex (V1)
Cochlear nucleus
Substantia gelatinosa

questions.explanation: The Nucleus Accumbens (part of the ventral striatum) is the primary target of VTA dopamine neurons for reward processing.

questions.question: According to Kent Berridge's model, what neurochemical system mediates 'liking' (hedonic sensory pleasure) rather than 'wanting'?

options.text: Endogenous opioids and cannabinoids in discrete hedonic hotspots
Mesolimbic dopamine exclusively
Thyroid hormone in the bloodstream
Acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions

questions.explanation: Consummatory 'liking' is mediated by mu-opioid and endocannabinoid signaling in localized hotspots of the NAc shell and ventral pallidum.

questions.question: In Wolfram Schultz's electrophysiological studies, what do midbrain dopamine neurons encode during associative learning?

options.text: Reward Prediction Error (the difference between expected and received reward)
The absolute brightness of visual stimuli
The pitch frequency of auditory tones
The precise body temperature of the animal

questions.explanation: Dopamine neurons signal Reward Prediction Errors: bursting for unexpected rewards, shifting to predictors, and pausing when rewards are omitted.

questions.question: What is the primary cellular mechanism of action of cocaine in the brain?

options.text: Blocking the presynaptic Dopamine Transporter (DAT), preventing dopamine reuptake
Directly activating postsynaptic GABA-A receptors
Destroying all acetylcholine receptors in muscle cells
Inhibiting the sodium-potassium ATPase pump

questions.explanation: Cocaine competitively blocks DAT, trapping dopamine in the synaptic cleft of the nucleus accumbens and causing persistent receptor stimulation.

questions.question: In addiction neurobiology, the transition from voluntary, goal-directed drug seeking to compulsive habit execution reflects a neural shift from:

options.text: The ventral striatum (Nucleus Accumbens) to the dorsal striatum (putamen)
The visual cortex to the auditory cortex
The spinal cord to the skull bone
The hippocampus to the pineal gland

questions.explanation: As drug use transitions to an automatic compulsive habit, control shifts anatomically from the ventral striatum to the dorsal striatum.

questions.question: What is 'Allostatic Load' as defined by neuroendocrinologist Bruce McEwen?

options.text: The cumulative systemic biological wear and tear resulting from chronic, unremitting stress adaptation
The maximum weight a human leg can lift before muscle tear
The number of action potentials a neuron can fire in one second
The total volume of cerebrospinal fluid in the spinal cord

questions.explanation: Allostatic load represents the physiological cost of chronic neuroendocrine activation (hypercortisolemia, sympathetic tone).

questions.question: Which limbic structure undergoes dendritic hypertrophy (expansion) and increased synaptic reactivity in response to chronic stress?

options.text: Basolateral complex of the Amygdala
CA1 field of the Hippocampus
Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex
Mammillary bodies

questions.explanation: While chronic stress atrophies hippocampal and prefrontal dendrites, it paradoxically expands dendrites in the amygdala, promoting chronic hyper-vigilance.

questions.question: What is the primary neurotrophic factor whose expression is severely decreased in the hippocampus during chronic stress and depression?

options.text: Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF)
Insulin-like Growth Factor 2
Epidermal Growth Factor
Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor C

questions.explanation: BDNF supports neuronal survival, dendritic branching, and synaptic plasticity; its reduction is a hallmark of depression pathophysiology.

questions.question: How does intravenous Ketamine produce rapid antidepressant effects within hours in treatment-resistant depression?

options.text: By antagonizing NMDA receptors, triggering a burst of glutamate that activates AMPA receptors and mTOR-dependent synaptogenesis
By permanently destroying serotonin reuptake transporters
By freezing dopamine release in the substantia nigra
By stimulating melatonin production during broad daylight

questions.explanation: Low-dose ketamine blocks NMDA receptors on GABAergic interneurons, causing rapid glutamate release, AMPA activation, and synaptogenesis via mTOR.

questions.question: What core circuit abnormality characterizes Generalized Anxiety Disorder and Panic Disorder in functional neuroimaging studies?

options.text: Hyperactive amygdala responsiveness coupled with deficient top-down inhibitory control from the ventromedial prefrontal cortex
Complete absence of blood flow to the occipital visual cortex
Total paralysis of all spinal alpha motor neurons
Excessive enlargement of the ventricles with no cortical changes

questions.explanation: Anxiety disorders reflect an imbalance: hyper-excitable bottom-up amygdalar threat signaling and impaired top-down prefrontal inhibition.

questions.question: Benzodiazepines (e.g., diazepam, lorazepam) exert rapid anxiolytic effects by acting as positive allosteric modulators at which receptor?

options.text: GABA-A receptors (increasing chloride channel opening frequency)
NMDA glutamate receptors
D2 dopamine receptors
Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors

questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines bind to a specific regulatory site on GABA-A receptors, facilitating GABA binding and increasing inhibitory chloride influx.

questions.question: In Schizophrenia, what dopaminergic abnormality is linked to positive symptoms such as auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions?

options.text: Hyperactivity of dopamine neurotransmission in the mesolimbic pathway
Total absence of dopamine in the substantia nigra
Destruction of dopamine receptors in the retina
Selective overproduction of dopamine in the cerebellum

questions.explanation: Mesolimbic dopamine hyperactivity is the primary driver of positive psychotic symptoms in schizophrenia, blocked by D2 antagonists.

questions.question: The NMDA receptor hypofunction hypothesis of Schizophrenia arose from the observation that which recreational drug produces symptoms mimicking schizophrenia?

options.text: Phencyclidine (PCP / 'Angel Dust') and Ketamine
Nicotine
Aspirin
Caffeine

questions.explanation: Non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonists like PCP and ketamine induce positive, negative, and cognitive symptoms mimicking schizophrenia.

questions.question: What is the primary neuroanatomical target of microelectrode arrays in invasive motor Brain-Computer Interfaces (e.g., BrainGate)?

options.text: Primary Motor Cortex (M1) on the precentral gyrus
Primary visual cortex (V1) in the occipital lobe
The pineal gland
The fourth ventricle choroid plexus

questions.explanation: Intracortical BCIs implant arrays into M1 to record single-unit and multi-unit motor action potentials for decoding motor intent.

questions.question: How do modern speech neuroprosthetics restore communication in paralyzed individuals who cannot speak (anarthria)?

options.text: By decoding neural activity from speech motor cortices into kinematic vocal tract movements and synthesized words in real time
By physically replacing the patient's vocal cords with mechanical titanium wires
By delivering electric shocks to the diaphragm to force air out
By connecting the optic nerve directly to a loudspeaker

questions.explanation: Speech neuroprosthetics use deep learning to translate cortical activity from speech motor areas into text and synthesized speech.

questions.question: What defines a 'Closed-Loop' Deep Brain Stimulation (Responsive Neurostimulation) system?

options.text: It continuously records local neural biomarkers and delivers electrical stimulation only when pathological activity is detected
It delivers high-voltage shocks at a constant, unvarying frequency 24 hours a day
It requires the patient to manually turn a hand crank to generate power
It works without any electrical current by using sound echoes

questions.explanation: Closed-loop systems monitor local field potentials dynamically, delivering adaptive stimulation only when needed (e.g., aborting a seizure).

questions.question: The ethical concept of 'Cognitive Liberty' in neuroethics refers to:

options.text: The fundamental human right to mental self-determination, cognitive privacy, and protection against unauthorized neural monitoring or manipulation
The freedom to purchase any computer hardware without paying taxes
The requirement that all college students major in neuroscience
The legal right to drive a vehicle while sleeping

questions.explanation: Cognitive liberty is the proposed human right ensuring mental autonomy and protecting neural data against unauthorized decoding or coercion.

questions.question: Which brain structure acts as an emotional 'accelerator', while the ventromedial prefrontal cortex acts as the 'brake'?

options.text: Amygdala
Corpus callosum
Occipital lobe
Cochlea

questions.explanation: The amygdala drives rapid emotional vigilance (accelerator), whereas the prefrontal cortex provides top-down regulatory inhibition (brake).

questions.question: How does repeated chronic exposure to drugs of abuse alter D2 dopamine receptor density in the human striatum?

options.text: It causes marked downregulation (decrease) of striatal D2 receptors, leading to chronic anhedonia and drug tolerance
It permanently increases D2 receptors by 1,000%
It converts all D2 receptors into voltage-gated potassium channels
Receptor density remains completely unchanged in all addiction cases

questions.explanation: Chronic hyperstimulation prompts homeostatic downregulation of postsynaptic D2 receptors, causing blunted responses to normal rewards.

questions.question: In the neurobiology of anxiety, high concentrations of GABA in the central nervous system generally produce:

options.text: Anxiolysis (reduction in anxiety) through widespread hyperpolarization and reduced neuronal excitability
Intense panic attacks and visual hallucinations
Rapid heart rate exceeding 200 beats per minute
Severe muscle spasticity and seizures

questions.explanation: GABA is the chief inhibitory neurotransmitter; increasing GABAergic tone dampens neural firing in limbic circuits, relieving anxiety.

questions.question: What is the primary role of the Prefrontal Cortex in the human brain's emotional regulatory network?

options.text: Exerting top-down cognitive reappraisal and context-dependent inhibition over subcortical limbic structures like the amygdala
Directly pumping blood through the ventricular chambers
Synthesizing myelin sheaths for peripheral nerves in the legs
Filtering high-frequency sound waves in the middle ear

questions.explanation: The PFC provides top-down cognitive control, modulating emotional reactivity and fear expression through descending inhibitory projections.
